derivations.claim:
By [A1], for any sequence $(A_n)$ of nonempty sets the family
$\mathcal F=\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ has a choice function $g$. The composite
$n\mapsto g(A_n)$ is an indexed selector, even if some sets $A_n$ repeat.
Thus [F1] holds and supplies the countable-choice premise in the quotient
circle definition [F2].

For one factor, [F2] makes each quotient interval $q(I)$ open because
$q$ is open, and $q|_I$ is injective because $I$ has length less than $1$.
Its inverse chart is continuous: $q|_I$ is a continuous open bijection onto
$q(I)$. These charts cover the circle. If two charts overlap, local lifts
differ by an integer; this integer is locally constant, so each transition
map is locally a translation and hence smooth. The charts therefore define a
smooth one-manifold without boundary compatible with the quotient topology.

Addition and inversion on one factor are smooth in these charts. Near any
pair of points, choose local real lifts $x,y$ and an output chart around their
sum; after shrinking the input intervals, the coordinate expression for
addition is $x+y$ plus one fixed integer. Near any point, choose local lifts
for it and its inverse; the coordinate expression for inversion is $-x$ plus
one fixed integer. Both expressions are smooth. With the group law already
given by [F2], this is a Lie group by [F6]. Its underlying circle is compact,
Hausdorff and connected by [F2] and [F3], and it is abelian by the quotient
addition law.

Iterate the binary product smooth-structure construction in [F5] over the
finite number $r$ of factors. Multiplication and inversion are componentwise
products of the smooth one-factor maps in step 2.1; iterating the binary
component criterion in [F5] makes both operations smooth. The finite product
is compact by [F3], connected by [F3], and abelian coordinatewise. It is
therefore a compact connected abelian Lie group, hence a torus by [F4], of
dimension $r$. The coordinate curves
$\gamma_i(s)=(0,\ldots,[s],\ldots,0)$ are smooth group homomorphisms by the
quotient charts and coordinate group law, so [F9] applies. Their derivatives
at zero form the coordinate basis of $T_0T$, and
$\gamma_i(s+1)=\gamma_i(s)$, so each has period one. For any $t\in\mathbb R$,
$s\mapsto\gamma_i(ts)$ is a smooth group homomorphism with initial derivative
$t e_i$; uniqueness in [F9] makes it $\gamma_{t e_i}$. Therefore
$\exp_T(t e_i)=\gamma_{t e_i}(1)=\gamma_i(t)$, as needed for the stated
normalization. For $r=0$, the empty product is the one-point Lie group and
these assertions hold with empty basis.

The circle has a finite CW structure with one vertex $[0]$ and one open
$1$-cell, the image of $(0,1)$; its characteristic interval has both
endpoints attached to that vertex. For $T$, index product cells by subsets
$J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$: coordinates in $J$ lie in the open $1$-cell and
all other coordinates equal $[0]$. Each cell is an open cube of dimension
$|J|$, its closure meets only cells indexed by subsets of $J$, and its
characteristic cube is the product of the factor characteristic intervals;
identify each closed cube with a closed disk of the same dimension. The map
$q^r:[0,1]^r\to T$ is a continuous surjection because every coordinate class
has a representative in $[0,1]$ by [F2]. If $K$ is closed in the cube,
then $K$ is compact, $q^r(K)$ is compact, and $q^r(K)$ is closed because $T$
is Hausdorff by [F2] and [F3]. Thus $q^r$ is a quotient map. It is the
characteristic map for the top cell. Every lower-cell characteristic cube is
obtained by precomposing $q^r$ with the continuous coordinate insertion that
fixes omitted coordinates at $0$, so the quotient topology of $q^r$ already
makes every characteristic map continuous; conversely $q^r$ is itself one of
those maps. Hence this quotient topology is exactly the weak topology
determined by the finitely many characteristic cubes. This gives a finite CW
structure with the identity as a $0$-cell. The singleton
identity is a subcomplex, so [F7] gives the homotopy extension property for
its inclusion.

The compact Hausdorff space $T$ is compactly generated: its identity map
from the compact Hausdorff space $T$ tests every open subset in the
compactly-generated topology. It is weak Hausdorff because every continuous
image of a compact Hausdorff space is compact and compact subsets of the
Hausdorff space $T$ are closed. Together with the cofibration from step 4.1,
[F8] shows that the based group is well-pointed.

derivations.claim: By [F6] and the group isomorphism [F7], the Milnor theorem's well-pointed CW-type hypothesis holds for the circle model used in each factor. The product of the $r$ free contractible circle models is free for the coordinatewise product action: if a tuple is fixed by $t=(t_1,\ldots,t_r)$, freeness in each coordinate gives $t_i=1$ for every $i$. It is contractible because a finite product of contractions is a contraction. The quotient map $E_{S^1}\to E_{S^1}/S^1$ is open, since the saturation of an open set is a union of its group translates. Its finite product is an open surjection whose fibers are exactly the $T$-orbits, hence is a quotient map and induces $BT\cong(BS^1)^r\cong(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r$ by [F1]. The assertion is immediate for the empty product $r=0$.

For each $n$, [F2] makes $H_{n-1}(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb Z)$ free. In [F3] with $G=\mathbb R$, its Ext term is therefore zero, so evaluation identifies $H^n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb R)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb Z),\mathbb R)$. The same sequence with $G=\mathbb Z$ identifies the integral class $u^k$ with a generator of the corresponding Hom group; naturality under $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ sends it to a nonzero generator. To check multiplication is preserved, put $X=\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}$, take $\varphi\in C^p(X;\mathbb Z)$ and $\psi\in C^q(X;\mathbb Z)$, and write $j\varphi$ for postcomposition with coefficient inclusion $j:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$. On each singular $(p+q)$-simplex $\sigma$, the front/back formula [F8] gives
$$(j\varphi\smile\,j\psi)(\sigma)=j(\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p]))\,j(\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q]))=j((\varphi\smile\psi)(\sigma)),$$
because $j$ preserves multiplication. Thus the cohomology coefficient map is a ring map and the image of $u^k$ is $u_{\mathbb R}^k$. Therefore $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb R)=\mathbb R[u_{\mathbb R}]$, with $|u_{\mathbb R}|=2$, and all odd groups vanish.

Apply [F4] to the integral singular chain complex of $\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}$ with $G=\mathbb R$. Each chain group is free over $\mathbb Z$; by [F2], every $H_{n-1}(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb Z)$ is free, so the Tor term vanishes. Hence $H_n(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty};\mathbb R)$ is $\mathbb R$ for even $n$ and zero for odd $n$, finite-free in each degree.

For $r\geq1$, apply [F5] to $(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^{r-1}\times\mathbb{CP}^{\infty}$, using the finite-free homology of the last factor established in step 1.3. Repeating this finite number of times identifies the product cohomology ring with the graded tensor product of $r$ copies of $\mathbb R[u_{\mathbb R}]$. Since each generator has even degree, the graded tensor-product signs are all positive; the result is $\mathbb R[u_1,\ldots,u_r]$. For $r=1$ this is step 1.2.

The symmetric algebra on the dual basis $e_1^*,\ldots,e_r^*$ is the polynomial algebra on those generators. Assigning each generator degree two and sending $e_i^*$ to the factor class $u_i$ from step 2.1 defines a bijective graded-algebra homomorphism. This is the stated identification, with the chosen product presentation fixing its normalization.

If $r=0$, $ET$ and $BT$ are the one-point space and $\mathfrak t=0$, so both rings are $\mathbb R$ in degree zero. AC is used only through [F2]–[F5]; no additional arbitrary choice is made in the finite product, the naturality maps, or the generator identification.

derivations.claim: The right diagonal action is a group action by homeomorphisms, so its orbit quotient $ET\times_T M$ is a topological space. By [F5]–[F7] its real singular cohomology has the stated cup-product ring structure; at $M=\{\ast\}$ the quotient is $BT$, whose coefficient ring is identified by [F1].

Pullback by each $a_{t^{-1}}$ preserves wedge products: evaluating on tangent vectors shows that pulling back the pointwise alternating product gives the product of the pullbacks. Thus the diagonal $T$-action is by algebra automorphisms and its fixed subspace is closed under the multiplication defined by the algebraic tensor-product rule and [F15]–[F16]. Since each polynomial generator has degree two, $d$ raises form degree by one, and contraction lowers form degree by one, both summands in $d_T$ raise total degree by one. By [F11] and [F12], each summand is a degree-one derivation because each $u_i$ has even degree. Under a change of basis of $\mathfrak t$, the polynomial basis and vector-field basis transform contragrediently; linearity in [F3] then makes $\sum_i u_i\otimes X_{e_i}$ basis-independent, so $d_T$ is unchanged.

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be any sequence of nonempty sets and let $\mathcal F=\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$. By [A1], choose a function $g$ on $\mathcal F$ with $g(S)\in S$ for every $S\in\mathcal F$. Then $c(n):=g(A_n)$ is a function on $\mathbb N$, including when different indices have equal sets, and $c(n)\in A_n$ for every $n$. This is exactly the indexed selector in [F17], so the countable-choice hypothesis of [F3] is satisfied.

Pullback naturality [F13] shows that $d$ preserves the $T$-fixed forms. For $t\in T$, the left action law and commutativity give $a_t\circ a_{\exp(-s e_i)}=a_{\exp(-s e_i)}\circ a_t$; differentiating at $s=0$ shows $(a_t)_*X_{e_i}=X_{e_i}$. By the pointwise definition [F9], contraction by each $X_{e_i}$ preserves invariant forms, while $u_i$ is fixed by the stipulated trivial action on the polynomial factor. Both terms therefore preserve the diagonal $T$-fixed subspace, so $d_T:C_T(M)\to C_T(M)$ is well-defined.

On polynomial-valued forms, expand the square as
$$d_T^2=d^2-\sum_i u_i(d\iota_{X_{e_i}}+\iota_{X_{e_i}}d)+\sum_{i,j}u_iu_j\iota_{X_{e_i}}\iota_{X_{e_j}}.$$
The first term is zero by [F8]. The last sum is zero because $u_i u_j=u_j u_i$ while insertions into alternating forms anticommute by [F9]. The middle sum is $-\sum_i u_i\mathcal L_{X_{e_i}}$ by [F14]. Hence $d_T^2\alpha=-\sum_i u_i\mathcal L_{X_{e_i}}\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in C_T(M)$.

Put $\phi_s=a_{\exp(-s e_i)}$. The local torus definition [F18] identifies $\exp(-s e_i)$ with the coordinate one-parameter subgroup, so the group law gives $\phi_{s+h}=\phi_s\circ\phi_h$. Differentiating at $h=0$ gives $\frac{d}{ds}\phi_s(p)=(d\phi_s)_pX_{e_i}(p)=X_{e_i}(\phi_s(p))$ by step 2.1. Thus $\phi_s$ is the flow of $X_{e_i}$. For an invariant form $\alpha$, $\phi_s^*\alpha=\alpha$ for every $s$; differentiating at zero and using [F10] gives $\mathcal L_{X_{e_i}}\alpha=0$. Substitution in step 2.2 proves $d_T^2\alpha=0$ on $C_T(M)$.

If $r=0$, the sum in $d_T$ is empty and $d_T=d$, whose square is zero by [F8]. If the action is trivial, every $X_{e_i}=0$ and again $d_T=d$ on invariant forms. If $M=\varnothing$, both the form complex and the Borel construction are empty, and [F19] makes its singular cohomology zero. No compactness of $M$, symplectic form, or Hamiltonian hypothesis was used.

derivations.claim: Define $\Phi([v,x])=v\cdot x$ from $ET\times_TT$ to $ET$, where $v\cdot x$ is the right Milnor action. It is well-defined because $\Phi([v\cdot h,x-h])=(v\cdot h)\cdot(x-h)=v\cdot x$. Its inverse is $v\mapsto[v,0]$: $\Phi([v,0])=v$, and the quotient relation gives $[v,x]=[v\cdot x,0]$. Both maps are continuous by the quotient topology and continuity of the group action, so this is a homeomorphism. By [F2], $ET$ is contractible; [F3] identifies its real singular cohomology with that of a point.

Integer translations preserve $dx$, so $-dx$ descends through the standard quotient charts to a global smooth one-form $\eta$ on the circle. The circle translations act transitively, so an invariant smooth function is constant. Every smooth one-form is $f(x)dx$ for a smooth periodic function $f$; invariance under all translations forces $f$ constant. Since higher forms vanish on a one-dimensional manifold, the invariant form algebra is spanned by $1$ and $\eta=-dx$. By [F7], the negative-exponential flow is $[x]\mapsto[x-s]$, hence $X_e=-\partial_x$ and $\iota_{X_e}\eta=1$; also $d\eta=0$. Substitution in [F1] gives $d_TP(u)=0$ and $d_T(P(u)\eta)=-uP(u)$.

A point has one singular simplex in each dimension. If $\sigma_n$ is its unique $n$-simplex, $\partial\sigma_n=(\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^j)\sigma_{n-1}$, whose coefficient is $1$ for even $n$ and $0$ for odd $n$. Thus $C^n(\{\ast\};\mathbb R)=\mathbb R$, and its coboundary $\delta^n$ is identity for odd $n$ and zero for even $n$. The cohomology quotient in [F4] is therefore $\mathbb R$ in degree zero and zero in every positive degree. Together with step 1.1 this proves the stated Borel cohomology.

Multiplication by $u$ is injective on $\mathbb R[u]$, so the differential from the odd summand $\mathbb R[u]\eta$ has zero kernel and image $u\mathbb R[u]$ in the even summand. Therefore Cartan cohomology is the quotient $\mathbb R[u]/u\mathbb R[u]\cong\mathbb R$ in degree zero and is zero in positive degrees, matching step 2.1. The constant polynomial $1$ survives, while every positive power $u^k$ is the boundary $-d_T(u^{k-1}\eta)$; no odd class survives.
